---
title: "Training models"
---

[pyreml]{.pyreml} fits linear mixed models by direct differentiation of the Restricted
Maximum Likelihood (REML) using [PyTorch](https://pytorch.org/) for variance parameter estimation.
It benefits from PyTorch parallelization and GPU acceleration.

## Fitting process

### The `fit` method

Once a [pyreml]{.pyreml} model is specified, it can be trained with the `.fit()` method.

```python
model.fit()
```

This runs the full pipeline, calling this series of methods: 

- `.OLS()`, [Ordinary least squares](#ols) (OLS) initialization of $\mathbf{\beta}$,

- `.REML()`, [REML](#reml) estimation of the variance components,

- `.HMME()`, [Henderson's mixed model equations](#hmme) (HMME) for the random-effect predictions.

REML and HMME are engaged whenever the model carries random effects, a residual variance structure,
or several responses; otherwise the fitting process stops at the OLS step.

### Numerical resolution

The `fit` method takes a `dtype` argument:

- `"mixed"` (default): OLS and a first REML pass run in `float32` to approach
the optimum cheaply, then a second REML pass and HMME run in `float64` to refine
the estimate and produce reliable outputs.

- `"double"`: all three steps (OLS, REML, HMME) run in `float64`
($=$ `torch.double`). This option is intended for GPUs optimized for `float64`
where the `float32` warm-up is not useful.

- `"float"`: all three steps run in `float32`. Fastest, but all outputs
are single-precision and in some cases the REML solver can go off-track badly.

## OLS

The fixed effects are first estimated by ordinary least squares,

$$
\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}_{\text{OLS}} =
(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y},
$$

implying $\mathbf{X}$ to be full-rank. If the model carries no random effect, an `iid` residual and a single response,
then the OLS solution is already the answer and training stops here.
Otherwise the OLS estimate initializes $\mathbf{\beta}$ before REML.
This initialization is always performed by `.fit()` and is strongly recommended
for lower level uses of [pyreml]{.pyreml}.

## REML

### REML loss

The per-effect blocks $\mathbf{G_a} = \mathbf{\Sigma_a} \otimes \mathbf{K_a}$
(see [Variance structures](variance_structures.qmd)) are assembled into the full
random-effect covariance by a direct sum over effects:

$$
\mathbf{G} = \bigoplus_\mathbf{a} \mathbf{G_a},
$$

and the marginal covariance of the observations follows as:

$$
\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{Z}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{Z}^\top + \mathbf{R}.
$$

Because observations may be missing in unbalanced designs,
$\mathbf{\Sigma_R} \otimes \mathbf{K_R}$
is assembled over all original rows and then restricted to the observed
entries through a residual “incidence” $\mathbf{W}$ such as:
$\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{W}\left(\mathbf{\Sigma_R} \otimes \mathbf{K_R}\right)\mathbf{W}^\top$.

The variance parameters and $\mathbf{\beta}$ are estimated by direct gradient descent of the
negative log-likelihood [@simchoni_integrating_2023], restricted (REML) so as to yield unbiased estimates of the variance
parameters [@patterson_recovery_1971; @harville_maximum_1977]:

$$
-2\ell_{\text{REML}} = \log\lvert\mathbf{V}\rvert
+ \mathbf{r}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}
+ \log\lvert\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}\rvert
+ (n - p) \log(2\pi),
$$

with $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{\beta}$.

### Optimization

The objective is optimized with L-BFGS [@liu_limited_1989] under a strong-Wolfe
line search, with Adam [@kingma_adam_2017] as a fallback for steps the line
search cannot complete. The variance parameters and $\mathbf{\beta}$ are
optimized jointly.

### SMW

The REML computation uses the Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury identity (SMW) [@MR38136]
which can have an important impact on the performance of the models
depending on their specification.

#### Interest of SMW for REML

The use of SMW aims at avoiding forming and inverting $\mathbf{V}$ directly:

$$
\begin{align}
\mathbf{V}^{-1}
    &= \left(\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{Z}^{\top} + \mathbf{R}\right)^{-1} \\
    &= \mathbf{R}^{-1}
    - \mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{Z}
   \mathbf{C}^{-1}
    \mathbf{Z}^{\top}\mathbf{R}^{-1},
\end{align}
$$

with the capacitance matrix $\mathbf{C}$:

$$
\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{Z}^{\top}\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{Z} + \mathbf{G}^{-1}.
$$

The associated determinant lemma gives the REML log-determinant without forming
$\mathbf{V}$ either:

$$
\log |\mathbf{V}|
    = \log |\mathbf{R}|
    + \log |\mathbf{G}|
    + \log |\mathbf{C}|.
$$

Therefore, the problem transposes from inverting $\mathbf{V}$ to inverting $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{R}$.

Using the properties of direct sum and Kronecker product:

$$
\mathbf{G}^{-1} = \bigoplus_\mathbf{a} (\mathbf{\Sigma_a}^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{K_a}^{-1}).
$$

For the residual (see [this section](variance_structures.qmd#the-residual)):

$$
\mathbf{R}^{-1} = \mathbf{W}\left(\mathbf{\Sigma_R}^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{K_R}^{-1}\right)\mathbf{W}^\top,
$$

which only stands under some conditions, including:

- if $\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{I}$;
- or if both $\mathbf{\Sigma_R}$ and $\mathbf{K_R}$ are diagonal, as 
$\mathbf{W}$ is a mere row-column selector.

Most left-hand and right-hand term inverses can be broken down even further, avoiding expensive computations for $\mathbf{G}^{-1}$ and $\mathbf{R}^{-1}$. The SMW path trades the complexity of inverting a dense $\mathbf{V}_{n \times n}$ for inverting a dense $\mathbf{C}_{q \times q}$ at each step.

#### Implementation of SMW

SMW is usually more efficient when $q < n$, with $q$
the number of columns of $\mathbf{Z}$
(the total dimension of $\mathbf{u}$) and $n$ the
number of stacked observations (*i.e.* $\mathbf{Z}$
is narrower than tall). Indeed, inverting the $q \times q$
matrix $\mathbf{C}$ is cheaper than inverting the $n \times n$ matrix
$\mathbf{V}$ only when $q < n$. 

[pyreml]{.pyreml} mostly conforms to this "dimensional rule",
selecting `SMW=True` when $q < n$, `SMW=False` otherwise.

However:

- using the high-level `from_dataframe` constructor, if the user
forces `SMW=True` or `False` then their decision takes precedence
over any other rule.
- using the high-level `from_dataframe` constructor, if all
of the following conditions are met then SMW is switched off
regardless of the dimensional rule:
    - $\mathbf{W} \neq \mathbf{I}$, which can arise for instance with several unbalanced options, or when using autoregressive structures.
    - the residual covariance $\mathbf{R}$ is not designed as a diagonal matrix.

Indeed, in this situation
$\mathbf{R}^{-1} \neq \mathbf{W}\left(\mathbf{\Sigma_R}^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{K_R}^{-1}\right)\mathbf{W}^\top$
and inverting the $n \times n$ matrix $\mathbf{R}$ is just as expensive as inverting
$\mathbf{V}$.

- with the low-level constructor:
    - if `varmeth_inv` only is provided, SMW is forced on;
    - if `varmeth` only is provided, SMW is forced off;
    - if both methods are available, the dimensional rule applies.


### Structured forward

Consider a random regression with three levels and four observations, an
intercept and a covariate $x$ being carried on each level:

$$
\newcommand{\z}{{\color{lightgray}0}}
\mathbf{Z_a} =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & \z & \z & x_1 & \z & \z\\
1 & \z & \z & x_2 & \z & \z\\
\z & 1 & \z & \z & x_3 & \z\\
\z & \z & 1 & \z & \z & x_4
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

$\mathbf{Z_a}$ can be entirely described by the pair
$(\mathbf{F_a}, s)$, defined as the values each observation carries and
the level it loads them on:

$$
\mathbf{F_a} =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & x_1\\ 1 & x_2\\ 1 & x_3\\ 1 & x_4
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
s = (1, 1, 2, 3).
$$

Row $i$ of $\mathbf{F_a}$ is written $\mathbf{f}_i$, and $s(i)$ is the level
loaded by observation $i$. Over several responses, $\mathbf{F_a}$ is
block-diagonal: each row carries the values of its own response, matching the
response blocks of $\mathbf{\Sigma_a}$.

Assembling $\mathbf{V_a} = \mathbf{Z_a}\mathbf{G_a}\mathbf{Z_a}^\top$
directly forms the Kronecker block
$\mathbf{G_a} = \mathbf{\Sigma_a} \otimes \mathbf{K_a}$, then
multiplies through every column of $\mathbf{Z_a}$. Yet each row of
$\mathbf{Z_a}$ being confined to a single level, entry $(i,j)$ of that
product reduces to the covariance between the values carried by
observations $i$ and $j$, scaled by the kernel entry between the levels
they load:

$$
[\mathbf{V_a}]_{ij} =
\mathbf{f}_i^\top\,\mathbf{\Sigma_a}\,\mathbf{f}_j\,
[\mathbf{K_a}]_{s(i)\,s(j)}.
$$

The right-hand factor collects into $\mathbf{K_a}$ read at the observed
level pairs:

$$
\left[\mathbf{K_a}^{\text{obs}}\right]_{ij} =
\left[\mathbf{K_a}\right]_{s(i)\,s(j)},
\qquad
\mathbf{K_a}^{\text{obs}} =
\begin{pmatrix}
K_{11} & K_{11} & K_{12} & K_{13}\\
K_{11} & K_{11} & K_{12} & K_{13}\\
K_{21} & K_{21} & K_{22} & K_{23}\\
K_{31} & K_{31} & K_{32} & K_{33}
\end{pmatrix},
$$

so that the whole contribution is written as a Hadamard (elementwise) product $\odot$:

$$
\mathbf{V_a} =
\left(\mathbf{F_a}\,\mathbf{\Sigma_a}\,\mathbf{F_a}^\top\right)
\odot \mathbf{K_a}^{\text{obs}}.
$$

Neither $\mathbf{G_a}$ nor $\mathbf{Z_a}\mathbf{G_a}\mathbf{Z_a}^\top$ is ever
formed, sparing both the memory and the time they would cost.
This was exemplified with random regression, but
holds for any effect built by `from_dataframe`. The full
covariance follows as $\mathbf{V} = \sum_\mathbf{a} \mathbf{V_a}$,
residual included.

On the [SMW](#smw) path, a second structured forward optimization is applied
to prevent the formation of $\mathbf{R}^{-1}$ and of the Kronecker block
$\mathbf{\Sigma_R}^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{K_R}^{-1}$ it is read from.
Any $\mathbf{Z}$, $\mathbf{X}$ or $\mathbf{r}$ column 
can be reshaped as a matrix $\mathbf{U}$ over the level $\times$ response grid:

$$
\mathbf{R}^{-1}\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{U})
= \operatorname{vec}\left(\mathbf{K_R}^{-1}\,\mathbf{U}\,\mathbf{\Sigma_R}^{-1}\right).
$$

The levels are contracted along the rows, the responses along the columns, and the
result is flattened back. Two small products replace one large inverse, which
is never formed. Unbalanced designs leave part of the grid empty, which is what the residual
incidence $\mathbf{W}$ encodes. Operands are therefore lifted onto the
complete grid, contracted, and read back at the observed cells afterwards.

The structured forward path is switched off when:

- using the `from_dataframe` high level builder, the user forces `structured_forward = False`;
- always when using the low level builder.

### Analytical backward

The REML gradient with respect to any variance parameter $\theta$ has a closed
form:
$$
\frac{\partial(-2\ell_{\text{REML}})}{\partial\theta} =
\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\mathbf{A}\,\frac{\partial\mathbf{V}}{\partial\theta}\right),
$$
$$
\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{V}^{-1} -
\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}\mathbf{r}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1} -
\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}
\left(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}\right)^{-1}
\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1},
$$

with $\partial(-2\ell_{\text{REML}})/\partial\mathbf{\beta} =
-2\,\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}$.
As $\mathbf{V} = \sum_\mathbf{a}\mathbf{V_a}$,
for a given random effect (or the residual), the trace permutes into:

$$
\frac{\partial(-2\ell_{\text{REML}})}{\partial\theta_\mathbf{a}} =
\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\mathbf{Z_a}^\top\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{Z_a}\;
\frac{\partial\mathbf{G_a}}{\partial\theta_\mathbf{a}}\right).
$$

$\mathbf{A}$ is therefore evaluated once at the current point and shared by
every variance parameter. Reusing the decomposition of
[structured forward](#structured-forward), where $\mathbf{Z_a}$ is replaced by
$(\mathbf{F_a}, s)$ and $\mathbf{G_a}$ by $\mathbf{\Sigma_a}$ and
$\mathbf{K_a}$, the trace contracts onto each variance matrix:

$$
\frac{\partial(-2\ell_{\text{REML}})}{\partial\mathbf{\Sigma_a}} =
\mathbf{F_a}^\top\left(\mathbf{A} \odot \mathbf{K_a}^{\text{obs}}\right)\mathbf{F_a},
\qquad
\left[\frac{\partial(-2\ell_{\text{REML}})}{\partial\mathbf{K_a}}\right]_{st} =
\sum_{\substack{i\,:\,s(i)=s \\ j\,:\,s(j)=t}}
\left[\mathbf{A} \odot
\mathbf{F_a}\mathbf{\Sigma_a}\mathbf{F_a}^\top\right]_{ij}.
$$

On the [SMW](#smw) path, $\mathbf{V}$ is never formed, so neither is
$\mathbf{A}$. The trace is then read in the level space, from
$\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Z}$ directly:

$$
\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{Z} - \left(\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}\right)\left(\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}\right)^\top - \left(\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}\right)\left(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}\right)^{-1}\left(\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}\right)^\top
$$
which uses 3 quantities the SMW projection already delivers through $\mathbf{C}$:

$$
\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{M} - \left(\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{Z}\right)\mathbf{C}^{-1}\left(\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{M}\right),
\qquad \mathbf{M} \in \{\mathbf{Z}, \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{X}\}
$$

PyTorch autograd is therefore disabled through the assembly and factorisation
of $\mathbf{V}$ ($\mathbf{C}$ on the SMW path). Automatic differentiation is
only left with the last step, from each variance matrix to its own
parameterization, and never traverses the Kronecker products.

The analytical backward path is switched off when:

- using the `from_dataframe` high level builder, the user forces `analytic_backward = False`;
- always when using the low level builder.

### Convergence criterion

Convergence is declared when two successive evaluations of $-2\ell_{\text{REML}}$
agree to within a tolerance $\tau$, the smallest difference in likelihood that
remains meaningful given both the numerical resolution of the evaluation and the
scale on which likelihoods are compared:

$$
\tau = \min\left(
  \tau_{\max},\;
  \lvert -2\ell_{\text{REML}} \rvert \cdot 10^{-\delta_\text{tot}}
\right),
\qquad
\delta_\text{tot} = \min\left(\delta_{\max},\;
  \delta_e - \left(\delta_{c} + \delta_{r} + \delta_{\kappa}\right)
\right).
$$

The restricted likelihood grows with the number of observations: the same
dataset measured twice as often returns a value roughly twice as large. A fixed
absolute threshold would therefore demand ever more significant digits as the
dataset grows, and eventually more than the computer can hold. Counting
significant digits keeps that demand constant. The budget starts from the
machine epsilon $e$ of the working precision $(\delta_e = -\log_{10}(e) \approx
15.65$ in `float64`, $\approx 6.92$ in `float32`) and is capped by the
conservative ceiling $\delta_{\max} = 10$. The three positive corrections count
digits that are certain to be noise: $\delta_c$ carries the cumulated
uncertainty of the elementary components the likelihood is summed from, while
$\delta_r$ and $\delta_\kappa$ address the inversion of the variance
$\mathbf{V}$ (or the capacitance $\mathbf{C}$ on the [SMW](#smw) path):
$\delta_r$ as a random walk over the many operations of the factorisation,
$\delta_\kappa$ as the information lost to the conditioning of the matrix. They
are amplification factors that compound, hence the sum. Each is a conservative
proxy, and $\delta_\text{tot}$ an estimate of the surviving resolution: no REML
step is spent refining a decimal that carries no information.

The digit budget is relative, but what makes a likelihood difference meaningful
is absolute: two models separated by
$\Delta$[AIC](#akaike-information-criterion) $= 2$ are considered
distinguishable. The ceiling $\tau_{\max} = 0.02$, one hundredth of that scale,
keeps the tolerance well below it. When the digit budget alone would push $\tau$
past $\tau_{\max}$, the noise floor of the evaluation has reached the scale at
which models are told apart: the fit is reported as degenerate, the tolerance is
clamped to $\tau_{\max}$, and convergence is denied.

The tolerance $\tau$ and the digit budget $\delta_\text{tot}$, $\delta_e$,
$\delta_{c}$, $\delta_{r}$ and $\delta_{\kappa}$ are returned in the
[logs](building_models.qmd#logs), where degenerate cases can be diagnosed.

## HMME

With the estimated variance components treated as known, the fixed and random
effects are obtained jointly from Henderson's mixed model equations [@henderson_best_1975]:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{X} & \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{Z} \\
\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{X} & \mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{Z}+\mathbf{G}^{-1}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} \hat{\mathbf{\beta}} \\ \hat{\mathbf{u}} \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{y} \\
\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{y}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Their solution gives the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) of
$\mathbf{\beta}$ and the best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) of
$\mathbf{u}$, in a single solve.

The same system also yields the error variances of the estimates and predictions.
See [Prediction](prediction.qmd) for the prediction error variance of
$\hat{\mathbf{u}}$.

## Akaike information criterion

Once the model is fitted, the Akaike information criterion (AIC) is computed in two different ways depending on
whether it was performed by `OLS` or `HMME`/`REML`. The AIC is available as attribute `AIC` and
the AIC method is recorded as `AIC_meth`. 

These two AICs should not be compared with each other. AIC computed post-OLS
is designed for the exploration of fixed effects with no variance structure, and
AIC computed post REML/HMME is designed for the investigation of the variance
structure with a fixed $\mathbf{X}$ (*i.e.* a fixed `formula` in the model
specification).

AIC post OLS is computed using the likelihood, from the unbiased residual variance $\sigma^2_R$:

$$
-2\ell_{\text{ML}} = n \log\left( \frac{n-p}{n} \sigma^2_R \right) + n + n \log(2\pi)
$$

and AIC post REML/HMME is computed using the restricted likelihood ($-2\ell_{\text{REML}}$). 

In both cases, AIC is obtained by the addition of twice the total number of parameters ($\beta$,
and all independent variance parameters).

## Monitoring

The fit can be followed through the REML objective recorded at each iteration and
a convergence flag, both exposed on the model.

| Accessor                    | Content                                          |
|-----------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| `model.opti_REML.loss`      | The REML objective at each iteration.            |
| `model.opti_REML.converged` | Whether the convergence criterion was met.       |
| `model.opti_REML.duration`  | Wall-clock time of the REML fit, in seconds.     |

L-BFGS drives the optimization and Adam steps in only to recover iterations the
line search cannot complete; occasional Adam steps near a difficult region of the
objective are expected.

As an illustration, the last iterations of an example model REML convergence:

```py
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.plot(model.opti_REML.loss)
plt.title("-2LogLik (REML)")
plt.show()
```
